card.title: Galaxy Core — The Heart of Gravity
card.description: The densest region where millions of stars orbit a supermassive black hole.

sections.heading: What is the Galactic Core?
sections.content: The galactic core is the rotational center of a galaxy, where stellar density reaches its peak. Our Milky Way's core harbors Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole.

sections.heading: Extreme Environment
sections.content: Star formation rates are high, radiation is intense, and gravitational forces dominate. Stars orbit at incredible speeds around the central mass.

sections.heading: Observable Features
sections.content: Dense star clusters, X-ray emissions, and gravitational lensing effects make the core a dynamic region for study.

card.title: Spiral Arm — Rivers of Stars
card.description: Density waves where stars, gas, and dust concentrate in elegant spiral patterns.

sections.heading: What are Spiral Arms?
sections.content: Spiral arms are regions of higher stellar and gas density that form distinct patterns in spiral galaxies. They're not static structures but density waves that stars pass through.

sections.heading: Star Formation Zones
sections.content: Arms are active regions of star formation due to compressed gas clouds. Young, bright blue stars illuminate these regions prominently.

sections.heading: Dynamic Structures
sections.content: Stars don't stay in arms forever—they enter and exit as they orbit. The arms persist as waves, not as fixed groups of stars.

card.title: Nebula — Cosmic Clouds of Creation
card.description: Vast clouds of gas and dust where new stars are born from collapsing material.

sections.heading: What is a Nebula?
sections.content: Nebulae are interstellar clouds of dust, hydrogen, helium, and ionized gases. They serve as stellar nurseries and remnants of stellar death.

sections.heading: Types of Nebulae
sections.content: Emission nebulae glow from ionized gas, reflection nebulae scatter starlight, and dark nebulae block background light.

sections.heading: Star Formation
sections.content: Gravitational collapse within dense nebula regions triggers star formation, creating new stellar systems over millions of years.

card.title: Black Hole — Gravity's Ultimate Triumph
card.description: A region where spacetime curves so extremely that nothing, not even light, can escape.

sections.heading: What is a Black Hole?
sections.content: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape from it. The boundary is called the event horizon.

sections.heading: Supermassive Scale
sections.content: Galactic centers host supermassive black holes with masses millions to billions times our Sun. They influence entire galaxies.

sections.heading: Detection Methods
sections.content: We detect black holes through gravitational effects on nearby stars, X-ray emissions from accretion disks, and gravitational waves.

card.title: Galactic Halo — The Invisible Crown
card.description: A spherical region of old stars, globular clusters, and dark matter surrounding the galaxy.

sections.heading: What is the Halo?
sections.content: The galactic halo is a roughly spherical region extending far beyond the visible disk, containing old stars and most of the galaxy's mass in dark matter.

sections.heading: Ancient Populations
sections.content: Halo stars are among the oldest in the galaxy, formed in the early universe. Globular clusters orbit through this region.

sections.heading: Dark Matter Dominance
sections.content: Most halo mass is invisible dark matter, detected only through gravitational effects on visible matter and galaxy rotation curves.

card.title: Dust Lanes — The Dark Ribbons
card.description: Dense concentrations of cosmic dust that obscure light and trace spiral structure.

sections.heading: What are Dust Lanes?
sections.content: Dust lanes are dark regions where microscopic particles of silicates, carbon, and ice absorb and scatter starlight, creating visible dark streaks.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.content: Dust grains are byproducts of stellar nucleosynthesis and supernova explosions, later incorporated into new star and planet formation.

sections.heading: Tracing Structure
sections.content: Dust lanes often mark spiral arms and help astronomers map galactic structure through infrared observations.
